fields.title: Vendor Lock-In
fields.keyTakeaway: Lock-in is created by prompt tuning and specific features, mitigated by an abstraction layer and independent evals, and the goal is to know the cost of switching, not to eliminate it.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: How expensive is it to switch model providers?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: [[vendor-lock-in|Vendor lock-in]] in AI builds up unnoticeably: prompts are tuned to a specific model, specific features are used, evals are calibrated. After a year, switching takes months instead of days.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: What creates lock-in, in increasing order:
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: *Call format.* Easy, an abstraction layer solves it. *Model-specific prompt tuning.* A prompt polished for one model works worse on another. Requires retuning and running evals. *Specific features.* Prompt caching, structured output, special modes — implemented differently. *Fine-tuned models.* Do not transfer. *Built-in provider tools.* Search, code execution — you will have to build these yourselves.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: **Abstraction layer** over calls. Cheap, done immediately. **Provider-agnostic evals.** Allow comparing candidates in hours. **Regular alternative checks.** Once a quarter, run evals on another provider. Provides both knowledge of switching costs and bargaining power. **Caution with proprietary features.** Use them, but know how to replace them.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: Product consideration: **lock-in is not always bad.** A specific feature providing a noticeable advantage can be worth the lock-in. It's bad when lock-in happens accidentally and no one knows its price.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: The abstraction layer was built immediately — calls go through our own interface.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: Once a quarter we run evals on two alternative providers. Takes a day, yields a "quality, price, latency" table for each function.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: The last run showed that for classification and rephrasing, an alternative provider is 40% cheaper at the same quality. We switched these two steps. For response generation, we stayed with the current one — the quality difference is 6% in its favor.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: We use prompt caching, knowing that the alternative handles it differently. Switching estimate — three days to retune the prompt assembly pipeline.
fields.sections/3/blocks/4/text: We intentionally have no fine-tuned models: that is the strictest form of lock-in, and prompts are working well enough for now.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: Complete independence from providers is expensive and usually doesn't pay off: it means giving up features that only one has. The goal is to know the switching cost, not to drive it to zero.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: Lock-in is created by prompt tuning and specific features, mitigated by an abstraction layer and independent evals, and the goal is to know the cost of switching, not to eliminate it.
